Butler
BUT-ler
noun
From the Old French bouteillier, the bottle-bearer, from bouteille, a bottle; hence the officer who has charge of the wine and presents the cup — in Egypt and Persia a post of great trust, since the king’s life passed through his hands.

Biblical Definition

The butler is the cupbearer, the officer who tasted and presented the king’s wine — a post held only by a man the king trusted with his life, and therefore a position near the throne. Pharaoh’s chief butler and chief baker both offended their lord and were put into the ward of the captain of the guard, into the very prison where Joseph was bound (Gen 40:1-3). One night each dreamed, and in the morning they were sad, and Joseph asked them why, and said, “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you” (Gen 40:8). The butler saw a vine with three branches budding, blossoming, and ripening into clusters which he pressed into Pharaoh’s cup; Joseph read it: within three days he would be restored (Gen 40:13). And so it fell out on Pharaoh’s birthday: the butler was restored to his butlership and gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand (Gen 40:21). Joseph had asked one thing — think on me when it shall be well with thee — and the chapter closes with the flattest sentence in Genesis: “Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him” (Gen 40:23). Two full years passed (Gen 41:1). Then Pharaoh dreamed, the magicians failed, and the butler said, “I do remember my faults this day” (Gen 41:9) — and Joseph was shaved and brought out to stand before Pharaoh at the exact hour that saved two nations from famine.

Webster 1828 Definition

A cupbearer; the servant who has charge of the wine and presents the cup to his lord. Pharaoh’s butler was restored, and forgat the man who read his dream.

expand to see more

BUTLER, a servant or officer in a great family, who has the care of the liquors and plate, and presents the cup.

Old French bouteillier, from bouteille, a bottle; the bottle-bearer.

In the courts of Egypt and Persia a place of high trust, being near the king’s person.

Pharaoh’s chief butler dreamed of the vine, and was restored to his butlership (Gen 40:9-21).

He forgat Joseph two full years, and remembered him at the appointed hour (Gen 40:23; 41:9).

Key Scripture

Gen 40:1 — "And it came to pass after these things, that the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker had offended their lord the king of Egypt."

Gen 40:13 — "Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thine head, and restore thee unto thy place: and thou shalt deliver Pharaoh's cup into his hand, after the former manner when thou wast his butler."

Gen 40:21 — "And he restored the chief butler unto his butlership again; and he gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand:"

Gen 40:23 — "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him."

Modern Corruption

Joseph’s prison is retold as a motivational parable — keep believing and your dream will come true — when the text is about a God who governs the memory of a forgetful servant.

expand to see more

The live misuse is the motivational hijacking of Genesis 39–41. Joseph is made the hero of perseverance, the prison is made a season of personal growth, and the moral is that your dream will come to pass if you keep your attitude right. Every part of that is out of joint with the text. Joseph is not waiting on a dream of his own; he is interpreting other men’s, and telling them plainly that interpretations belong to God. He does not rise by attitude; he rises because a butler’s memory failed for exactly two years and then recovered at exactly the moment Pharaoh dreamed. And the account’s own summary is not a maxim about believing in yourself but a doctrine of God: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive (Gen 50:20). Prosperity preaching needs the story to be about Joseph. Scripture insists that it is about the LORD, who was with him in the pit, in Potiphar’s house, and in the prison, and who had the famine, the granaries, and the survival of the covenant family in view the whole time.

Recover the doctrine of providence at the point where it is hardest to feel — the delay. Joseph asked the butler for one favour, and got nothing for seven hundred days. It looked like the last door closing. In fact the forgetting was as much God’s work as the remembering, for had the butler spoken in the first week, Joseph would have been released as a favour to a foreign slave and vanished. He was kept in irons until the hour when the throne itself needed him, and then he went from the dungeon to the second chariot in a single day. That is not coincidence retrofitted with piety; it is the ordinary manner of God’s government, who upholdeth, directeth, disposeth, and governeth all creatures and things, from the greatest even to the least, by His most wise and holy providence (LBCF 5.1). The believer whose case has been forgotten by every man who promised to speak for him should mark the two years and the two dreams, and remember that the delay had a calendar.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The king’s cupbearer; restored on the third day, and forgetful two years, that God’s hour might be kept exactly.

expand to see more

Butler — Old French bouteillier, the bottle-bearer; the cupbearer of a great house.

Hebrew mashqeh, one who gives drink, a cupbearer (Gen 40:1; cf. Neh 1:11 of Nehemiah).

The vine with three branches: three days to restoration (Gen 40:12-13).

The one favour Joseph asked was forgotten for two full years (Gen 40:23; 41:1).

“I do remember my faults this day” — the memory returned on God’s schedule (Gen 41:9).

Usage

"The butler’s forgetting was as providential as his remembering — the delay had a calendar."

"Do not interpretations belong to God? Joseph disowns the gift before he uses it."

"A cupbearer’s trust was his master’s life; hence his nearness to the throne."
